sections.heading: Fun fact: this is how marks become grades
sections.body: When a teacher turns '8 out of 40' into a percentage, they are doing exactly this. It lets them compare a test out of 40 with one out of 60 fairly - the percentage puts everything on the same 0-100 scale.

questions.question: Sam spent 30% of his savings and that came to exactly GBP 60. How much did he have to start with?

hint.title: Working Backwards from a Percentage
hint.subtitle: Know the part and its percent? Climb to the whole.

sections.heading: The puzzle in reverse
body: Normally you find a percentage OF a known total. Here it is flipped: you know that 30% is GBP 60, and you want the original whole (100%).
The staircase trick: get down to 10% first, because from 10% you can build any percentage - including the full 100%.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 30% is GBP 60. So 10% is a third of that: 60 ÷ 3 = 20. Then 100% is ten lots of 10%: 20 x 10 = 200.

visual.title: Check it: 30% of 200
visual.tip: Set 30% of 200 and confirm it lands on 60 - that proves 200 is the whole.

sections.note: Step DOWN to 10%, then UP to 100%. 10% is the master key.

sections.heading: See it on different numbers
sections.body: If 20% is GBP 30, what is the whole?

sections.heading: Fun fact: detectives and scientists work backwards too
sections.body: Reversing a calculation - knowing the result and finding the start - is one of the most powerful moves in all of maths and science. It is how astronomers weigh planets they can never visit: they measure an effect and work backwards to the cause.
sections.note: Working backwards from a clue to the cause is a core trick of real scientists.

questions.question: A pizza is cut into 64 tiny squares. You eat 12.5% of it. How many squares is that?

hint.title: 12.5%: The Tricky One That's Really One Eighth
hint.subtitle: Some 'decimal' percentages are friendly fractions in disguise.

sections.heading: Don't panic at the decimal
body: 12.5% looks scary because of the .5, but it is secretly a very friendly fraction.
12.5% = 12.5/100 = 1/8. So finding 12.5% just means splitting into 8 equal parts.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 12.5% of 64 = one eighth of 64 = 64 ÷ 8 = 8. (Or halve, halve, halve: 64 -> 32 -> 16 -> 8.)

visual.tip: Shade 1 of 8 slices: 1/8 = 12.5%.

questions.question: A plant grew from 40 cm to 50 cm. By what percentage did its height increase?

hint.title: Percentage Change: How Much It Grew
hint.subtitle: Compare the change to where you STARTED.

sections.heading: Percentage change is always 'out of the start'
body: When something grows or shrinks, we measure the change as a percentage of the ORIGINAL amount - not the new one.
First find how much it changed, then ask 'what percentage of the start is that?'

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: 40 cm to 50 cm: the change is 50 - 40 = 10 cm. As a fraction of the start: 10/40 = 1/4 = 25%. So it grew by 25%.

visual.title: The change over the start
visual.tip: 10 out of 40 is the growth: 10/40 = 1/4 = 25%.

sections.note: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) turned into a percent.

sections.heading: See it on different numbers
sections.body: A price rises from 20 to 25.

sections.heading: Fun fact: a 50% fall does NOT undo a 50% rise
sections.body: If GBP 100 rises 50% to 150, then falls 50%, you get 75 - not back to 100! Because the fall is taken from the bigger number. Percentage change always depends on what you start from.
sections.note: Percentage rises and falls don't cancel, because each is measured from a different starting amount.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
sections.body: Change is reported as a percent.
points: Price rises and falls.
Population growth.
Getting faster: improving a race time.

questions.question: A GBP 100 jacket goes UP 20% in winter, then is cut DOWN 20% in the sale. What is the final price?

hint.title: The Up-Then-Down Trap
hint.subtitle: Two equal percentages do NOT cancel out. Here's why.

sections.heading: It feels like it should return to 100
body: Up 20%, then down 20% - surely that lands back at the start? It's the great percentage trap, and the answer is no.
The reason: each percentage is taken from a DIFFERENT amount. The rise is on 100, but the fall is on the bigger number.

sections.heading: The big idea
sections.body: Start GBP 100. Up 20%: 100 + 20 = 120. Now down 20%, but 20% of 120 = 24, so 120 - 24 = 96. You end at GBP 96, not 100.

visual.title: Up then down, step by step
visual.teachingPoint: The fall is bigger than the rise because it comes off a bigger number.

sections.note: Do it in two steps. The second percentage acts on the NEW amount, not the original.

sections.heading: See it on different numbers
sections.body: GBP 50, up 10% then down 10%.
steps: You end at GBP 49.50 - just under the start.

sections.heading: Fun fact: this trap fools grown-ups all the time
sections.body: Shops sometimes raise a price then advertise the same percentage 'off', and shoppers assume it's the original price - but it's actually a little lower OR the maths hides a smaller saving. Knowing this protects your money for life.
sections.note: An equal rise then fall always lands BELOW the start - a fact many adults get wrong.

sections.heading: Where it shows up
sections.body: Two-step percentage changes.
points: Prices up then discounted.
Investments that gain then lose.
Populations rising then falling.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body: Always do it in two separate steps:
points: GBP 200 up 10% then down 10%.
GBP 80 up 25% then down 25%.
Notice you always end below where you started.

sections.heading: Now back to your question
sections.body: GBP 100, up 20%, then down 20%.
sections.note: Do it in two steps. First add 20% to get the winter price, THEN take 20% off THAT new price - not off the original 100.
